title: Amenorrhoea
subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Amenorrhoea is the absence of menstrual bleeding for at least three cycles or 12 weeks in a woman of reproductive age. It requires systematic assessment of physiological, anatomical and systemic causes, especially those common in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Amenorrhoea is defined as no menstrual flow for ≥3 consecutive months in a previously menstruating woman (secondary) or no menses by age 15 with normal secondary sexual characteristics (primary). Diagnosis starts with a focused history and basic examination.
b: Ask about age of menarche, cycle pattern, pregnancy possibility, stress, weight change, medications, and systemic symptoms.
Physical exam: assess BMI, signs of virilisation, thyroid, galactorrhoea, and pelvic exam for anatomical obstruction.

sections.p: Severity is graded by duration and impact on health (e.g., bone density loss, infertility). Staging follows the WHO classification for reproductive health: mild (≤6 weeks), moderate (6 weeks–6 months), severe (>6 months or complications).
b: Mild: often functional, reversible.
Moderate: may need hormonal work‑up.
Severe: risk of osteopenia, requires urgent investigation.

sections.p: Causes are grouped into endocrine, anatomical, systemic disease and iatrogenic categories. In East African low‑resource settings, infectious and nutritional causes are common.
b: Endocrine: pregnancy, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease, polycystic ovary syndrome.
Anatomical: Asherman's syndrome, cervical stenosis, uterine synechiae after curettage.
Systemic/infectious: HIV, TB (pelvic), malaria‑related weight loss, schistosomiasis, severe anemia.
Iatrogenic: hormonal contraceptives, chemotherapy, long‑term glucocorticoids.

sections.p: Patients report missed periods, often with associated symptoms that clue to the aetiology.
b: Pregnancy: positive urine test, breast tenderness.
Hyperprolactinaemia: galactorrhoea, headache.
PCOS: hirsutism, acne, obesity.
Asherman's: history of D&C, scant or absent flow, normal secondary sexual characteristics.

t.b: Is pregnancy present? Positive → manage as obstetric case; negative → continue work‑up.
Is hyperprolactinaemia present? Elevated → MRI pituitary if available; treat with bromocriptine if MRI not possible.
Is thyroid dysfunction present? Abnormal → treat hypo‑ or hyper‑thyroidism.
Is ovarian failure likely? High FSH/LH with low estradiol → primary ovarian insufficiency.
Is there uterine synechiae, ovarian cysts, or uterine mass? Findings guide surgical vs medical management.
Is HIV infection present? Positive → consider opportunistic infections, endocrine effects.
Is severe anemia present? Low Hb/ferritin may explain functional hypothalamic suppression.

b: Severe abdominal pain with fever → pelvic infection or abscess.
Rapid weight loss, vomiting → eating disorder or severe systemic disease.
Signs of hypovolaemia (pallor, tachycardia) → consider massive bleeding from uterine pathology.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; provide hormonal support when needed; monitor bone health and fertility goals.
b: Pregnancy: obstetric care.
Hyperprolactinaemia: dopamine agonist (bromocriptine) – avoids estrogen‑dependent tumour growth.
Thyroid disease: levothyroxine or antithyroid drugs – restores normal HPO axis.
Asherman's syndrome: hysteroscopic adhesiolysis; give estrogen‑progesterone sequential therapy to prevent re‑scarring.
PCOS: weight loss, metformin (if glucose intolerance) – improves insulin resistance, not first‑line hormonal therapy.
Severe anemia: transfusion if haemodynamically unstable, iron supplementation thereafter.

sections.p: Re‑evaluate menstrual return, bone density, and psychosocial impact.
b: Repeat β‑hCG after 2 weeks if initial test negative but suspicion remains.
Check serum prolactin and thyroid function after treatment of identified cause.
Bone mineral density scan after >12 months of amenorrhoea in women <30 years.
Oligomenorrhoea (infrequent periods) – cycles >35 days but still present.
Polymenorrhoea (frequent periods) – cycles <21 days.
Metrorrhagia (irregular bleeding) – bleeding between cycles, not absence.
Serum prolactin can be transiently elevated by stress; repeat after 30 min if borderline.
TSH may be normal in early central hypothyroidism; consider free T4.

faq.a: Yes, during pregnancy, lactation, or after menopause; otherwise it signals an underlying disorder.

faq.q: Why is a pregnancy test the first test?
faq.a: Pregnancy is the most common cause of missed periods and requires urgent obstetric management.
Intra‑uterine adhesions usually after curettage that block endometrial shedding, causing secondary amenorrhoea.

exam: A 22‑year‑old woman presents with 4 months of missed periods, hirsutism and BMI = 32 kg/m² — what is the most likely diagnosis and first investigation? — PCOS; obtain serum testosterone and LH/FSH ratio after ruling out pregnancy.

A patient with a history of D&C for incomplete miscarriage now has amenorrhoea for 6 months — which condition should you suspect and how would you confirm it? — Asherman's syndrome; perform pelvic ultrasound and consider hysteroscopy.
In a woman with HIV on antiretroviral therapy, amenorrhoea persists for 8 months — which endocrine abnormality is common and what test is indicated? — Hyperprolactinaemia; serum prolactin level.

A 30‑year‑old with severe anemia (Hb = 6 g/dL) and amenorrhoea for 3 months — what is the pathophysiological link and immediate management? — Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea from energy deficiency; transfuse if unstable, start iron therapy.

How would you manage amenorrhoea caused by a pituitary macroadenoma when MRI is unavailable? — Treat presumptive hyperprolactinaemia with bromocriptine and refer for surgical evaluation if visual symptoms develop.

A woman reports amenorrhoea after starting depot medroxyprogesterone acetate — what counselling should you give? — Explain that hormonal contraception suppresses ovulation and menses; reassure that fertility returns after discontinuation.
What red‑flag symptom in a patient with amenorrhoea mandates urgent referral? — Acute pelvic pain with fever suggesting pelvic infection or abscess.
Why is estrogen‑progesterone sequential therapy given after hysteroscopic adhesiolysis? — To promote endometrial regeneration and prevent re‑adhesion formation.
